old: we made sure it had been the death of us
new: we felt sure it had been the death of us
reason: False friend with a dead sense. In current English 'make sure' means 'ensure' or 'check', so the men's plea first reads as though they had ensured their own deaths. That is nonsense and forces a re-read, and the reader recovered only by recognizing the old idiom. Butler means 'we felt certain' (Greek 9.496 kai de phamen autoth' olesthai, 'and we thought we were lost then and there'). 'felt sure' keeps Butler's own 'sure' and is his own phrase for this sense elsewhere in the poem (PG #1727 line 9799, 'he felt sure it was Minerva'), so it restores rather than paraphrases (D29). 'had been' and 'the death of us' are unchanged. The meaning is recoverable from context, hence optional. Consistency note: accepted Book 4 prints Butler's 'made sure' unchanged twice (4.54, 4.57), where the 'ensure' reading is if anything more tempting ('we had made sure that it would come to nothing'). If the lead adopts this, those two belong to the same class; if the lead prefers edition-wide sameness, rejecting this one is defensible, because here the context forces the right reading.
